This is a hobby research site. The point is not to find a winning strategy; it is
to ask a question carefully enough that the answer can be trusted, whichever way it
comes out.

## Baselines come first

Before any model is built, the simplest possible answers are measured: for example
"it always goes up" or "it does what it did yesterday". A model only counts as
working if it beats those. A clever model that loses to a one-line rule has not
found anything.

## Every number comes with its uncertainty

A single figure such as "52% accuracy" says little on its own. Each result is shown
with a 95% confidence interval: the range the true value plausibly lies in, given
how much data there is. When two things are compared, the interval is on their
difference, and if that interval includes zero the honest reading is "no detectable
difference".

## Negative results are results

If nothing beats the baseline, that is the finding, and it is published as plainly
as a positive one would be. Results are not rerun with different settings until
something looks good. Model settings are fixed before the test is run.

## No peeking at the future

The most common way to fool yourself with market data is to let information from
the future leak into a decision made in the past. Here:

- A model making a call for a given day is trained only on days before it.
- Testing is "walk-forward": the model is trained on the past, makes its calls for
  the next stretch, then is retrained with that stretch added, and so on through
  history.
- The code has tests that deliberately corrupt all later data and check that
  earlier calls do not change. If they did, the test fails.

## Costs are included

Simulated results charge a cost every time a position changes. A rule that looks
good only when trading is free is not good.

## Backtests flatter; the live log decides

A test on history is where approaches get compared, so it tends to favour whatever
was tried. The stronger evidence is a live record: predictions written down before
the event and scored afterwards.

The live prediction log on this site can only be added to. Each entry carries a
fingerprint of the entry before it, so changing or removing an earlier entry is
detectable. A prediction must be written before the market opens for the day it is
about, and whether it was right is recorded separately once that day is over.

## What is published

Results, summary figures and the prediction log. Raw price and market data are not
published. Simulated returns appear only as summary figures.

## What this site is not

It is not advice, it does not trade, and it does not issue signals. See the
[disclaimer](disclaimer.qmd).
